Learning AI and machine learning from scratch

A free 15-stage path to learn AI and machine learning from scratch, from Python and math to LLMs and agentic AI.

How to use this guide

The guide has fifteen stages, from Python and basic math to language models (like ChatGPT or Gemini), AI agents and choosing a direction, and you go through it at your own pace. It assumes nothing beyond what you already know from high school: C, algorithms and math.

A few words you will see everywhere: artificial intelligence (AI) is the broad field of programs that do things we associate with thinking. Machine learning (ML) is the part of AI where the program is not given rules written by a person, but learns on its own from examples. Deep learning is the part of ML that uses large neural networks, and language models (LLMs) are its best-known results. Training a model means showing it many examples and gradually adjusting its parameters until it makes as few mistakes as possible.

Why this order

  1. Python and the tools: the language almost everything in AI is written in.
  2. Math: linear algebra, derivatives and probability are the language every model is explained in.
  3. Classical machine learning, fundamentals: the first models you train yourself and the ideas that apply to everything that follows (training, testing, overfitting).
  4. Classical machine learning, in depth: real, messy data, more types of models, serious evaluation.
  5. Neural networks: how a network learns, written by you from scratch, then with PyTorch.
  6. Deep learning in depth: the tricks that make large networks train well.
  7. Transformers: the architecture behind language models, built by you.
  8. How an LLM is trained: every phase, from raw text to an assistant that reasons.
  9. Generative and multimodal models: how images, sound and video are generated.
  10. Reinforcement learning: learning by trial and error, also used to train LLMs.
  11. LLM applications: how to build products on top of existing models.
  12. Agentic AI: models that use tools and carry out multi-step tasks on their own.
  13. MLOps and production: how a model gets used by real people.
  14. Ethics, safety and interpretability: the risks, and how to understand what happens inside a model.
  15. Choosing a direction: you try each type of AI job and pick what to focus on next.

Stages 1-8 are done in order. Stage 9 can be done any time after Stage 7, Stage 10 any time after Stage 6, and 11-14 after Stage 8. If you want to get to agents as fast as possible, the shortest path is 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 12, and you fill in the rest afterwards.

How each stage is structured

  • a short explanation: what you learn and why it matters;
  • numbered steps: you follow them in order, top to bottom, and each one links to a video, a course or an exercise;
  • "If something is unclear": backup explanations, only for when you need them;
  • the goal: what you should be able to do before moving on.

A few tips

  • Order matters more than speed. There is no rush to finish a stage. Before you start, also read the last section, Good habits and communities.
  • After every video or lesson, write the code you saw on your own, without copy-pasting. Practice helps more than another video.
  • You do not need a powerful laptop. Anything that needs a GPU runs for free in the browser, on Google Colab or Kaggle.
  • Use an AI assistant as a teacher, not to do your homework: ask it to explain what you did not understand in a different way, not to give you the solution.
  • All resources in the steps are free; some only require an account.
  • If you have already done Stage 3 of the cybersecurity guide, you know Python: in Stage 1 here, skip straight to step 3.

Stage 1Python and the tools

Python is the language almost everything in AI is written in: the libraries for data, for machine learning and for neural networks are all made for it. Since you already know C, you have the concepts (variables, loops, functions); you only learn the syntax and what is different. In the second part of the stage you learn the tools for working with data: notebooks, NumPy and pandas.

Steps, in order

  1. First contact with Python. Harvard's free CS50P course, Lecture 0 (Functions, Variables).
  2. The rest of the basics. Also from CS50P, the lectures Conditionals, Loops, Exceptions, Libraries and File I/O, each with its problem set.
  3. Notebooks, where you will work from now on. A notebook is a document where you alternate pieces of code with text and see the result right below each piece. Open Google Colab (Google account), go through the welcome notebook and run every cell.
  4. NumPy, the library for computing with vectors and matrices, which all the others build on. The official guide NumPy: the absolute basics for beginners, with every example run in Colab. You will see that an operation on a whole vector is written without a loop, unlike in C.
  5. pandas, the library for data tables (like Excel in code). The Pandas course on Kaggle Learn (free account, the exercises run in the browser).
  6. Charts, so you can look at the data before training anything on it. The Data Visualization course on Kaggle Learn.
  7. Git and GitHub, where you will keep your notebooks and projects. The interactive exercise Introduction to GitHub.
  8. Mini-project. Pick a dataset that interests you from Kaggle Datasets (sports, movies, weather), load it with pandas and answer five questions about it in a notebook, each with a chart.

If something is unclear

  • Python, slower and with short exercises: the Python course on Kaggle Learn.
  • NumPy and pandas, explained at length: the free book Python Data Science Handbook, chapters 2 and 3.

Goalthe mini-project on GitHub and being able to load, filter and chart any data table without looking up every command.

Stage 2The math you need

A machine learning model is, at heart, a mathematical function with many parameters, and training means finding the parameters for which the error is smallest. You need three things: linear algebra (data and parameters are vectors and matrices), derivatives (they show which direction to change the parameters in) and probability (models say how confident they are). The aim is not to write proofs, but to understand what is going on when you read a formula.

Steps, in order

  1. Vectors and matrices, intuitively. The Essence of linear algebra playlist by 3Blue1Brown: the first four videos (vectors, linear combinations, linear transformations, matrix multiplication) and the one on the dot product (Dot products and duality).
  2. Derivatives again, but seen differently than in high school. The Essence of calculus playlist, the first four videos. The most important part is the chain rule: the way neural networks learn, in Stage 5, is built on it.
  3. Derivatives for functions of several variables, meaning the gradient. From the Multivariable calculus course on Khan Academy, only the lessons on partial derivatives and the gradient. In short: the gradient is a vector that points in the direction in which the function increases fastest.
  4. How the gradient is used to find the minimum of a function. Video: Gradient Descent, Step-by-Step (StatQuest). Almost every model in this guide is trained this way.
  5. Probability, interactively. Seeing Theory, the chapters Basic Probability, Compound Probability and Probability Distributions: every idea has an animation you can play with.
  6. Basic statistics. The Statistics Fundamentals playlist (StatQuest): the videos on histograms, distributions, mean and variance, and the normal distribution.
  7. Bayes' theorem, meaning how you change your mind when new evidence appears. Video: Bayes theorem, the geometry of changing beliefs.
  8. All of it in code. In a notebook, with NumPy: multiply two matrices with three loops, as in C, and check the result with @; compute the derivative of a function approximately, with (f(x+h) - f(x)) / h; then write a gradient descent that finds the minimum of f(x) = (x - 3)² starting from x = 0, and plot how it gets closer to 3.

If something is unclear

  • Any probability or statistics concept, with exercises: Statistics and probability on Khan Academy.
  • If you prefer reading and want more rigor: the free book Mathematics for Machine Learning, chapters 2 (linear algebra), 5 (vector calculus) and 6 (probability). It is a reference, not something to read cover to cover.

Goalthe notebook from step 8 on GitHub and being able to explain, in your own words, what a gradient is and why gradient descent reaches the minimum.

Stage 3Classical machine learning, fundamentals

This is where you train your first models, on real data. The basic idea: you give the model many examples for which you know the answer (for example, houses with their size and price), it learns the relationship between them, and then you test it on examples it has not seen. The models in this stage (regression, decision trees) are simpler than neural networks, but companies still use them to solve a great many problems, and the ideas you learn here (training set and test set, overfitting, evaluation) apply to everything that follows.

Steps, in order

  1. The big picture. Video: A Gentle Introduction to Machine Learning (StatQuest).
  2. The basic concepts, with animations and exercises. Google's free Machine Learning Crash Course, the modules Introduction to ML, Linear regression, Logistic regression and Classification, then the three modules in the Data section (numerical data, categorical data, datasets, generalization and overfitting).
  3. Each model, explained in detail. The StatQuest videos, in order: Linear Regression, Logistic Regression, Decision and Classification Trees, Random Forests.
  4. How you know whether a model is good. The videos Bias and Variance, Cross Validation and The Confusion Matrix. In short: a model that memorized the examples instead of learning the rule is perfect on the training data and poor on new data. That is overfitting.
  5. Your first models in code, with scikit-learn, the standard library for classical ML. The Intro to Machine Learning course on Kaggle Learn, from start to finish.
  6. How to work with real data, which has missing values and text columns. The Intermediate Machine Learning course on Kaggle Learn. Near the end you get to XGBoost, the model that wins many competitions on tabular data; the idea behind it is in Gradient Boost Part 1.
  7. Unsupervised learning: the model only gets data and looks for groups in it on its own. The videos K-means clustering and Principal Component Analysis (PCA), then the K-means example from the scikit-learn documentation, run in Colab.
  8. Your first competitions. On Kaggle, submit a solution to Titanic (who survived) and to House Prices (the price of a house). Then, to see that it is not magic, write linear regression from scratch in NumPy, with the gradient descent from Stage 2, and compare the result with scikit-learn's.

If something is unclear

  • Any other model or concept: the StatQuest Machine Learning playlist has a video for almost every one.
  • A full, slower course with assignments: Machine Learning Specialization (Andrew Ng, Coursera). Enrolling is free; the certificate is paid.

Goala solution submitted to both Titanic and House Prices, linear regression from scratch on GitHub, and being able to explain what overfitting is and how you spot it.

Stage 4Classical machine learning, in depth

In practice, most of the work is not choosing the model, but preparing the data and evaluating the results correctly. In this stage you learn to work with data the way it comes from companies (incomplete, stored in databases, changing over time), get to know the rest of the classical models and learn to pick the right metric. This is also where you learn to explain why a model made a particular decision.

Steps, in order

  1. SQL, the language of databases, where most company data comes from. The Intro to SQL course on Kaggle Learn.
  2. Data cleaning: missing values, wrong formats, inconsistent text. The Data Cleaning course on Kaggle Learn.
  3. Feature engineering, meaning turning raw data into columns the model can learn from more easily. It often matters more than the model you choose. The Feature Engineering course on Kaggle Learn.
  4. The rest of the classical models. The StatQuest videos: K-nearest neighbors, Naive Bayes, Support Vector Machines, XGBoost and Ridge Regression (regularization, meaning penalizing models that are too complicated). After each one, try it in scikit-learn: the classification models on Titanic, Ridge on House Prices.
  5. Metrics. The video ROC and AUC, then the Metrics and scoring page in the scikit-learn documentation. An example of why this matters: a test for a rare disease that always says "healthy" is 99% accurate, but useless.
  6. Choosing a model's settings automatically (hyperparameter tuning). The Tuning the hyper-parameters page in scikit-learn, with the GridSearchCV and RandomizedSearchCV examples run on your House Prices model.
  7. Time series, meaning data that changes over time (sales, weather, traffic). The Time Series course on Kaggle Learn.
  8. Recommender systems, like the ones at Netflix or YouTube. Google's Recommendation Systems course.
  9. Why the model decided what it did. The Machine Learning Explainability course on Kaggle Learn (column importance, SHAP values).
  10. Full project. Take a new dataset from Kaggle and carry everything through from start to finish in a single notebook: cleaning, feature engineering, three different models compared with cross validation, tuning, the right metric and an explanation of the final model's decisions.

If something is unclear

  • Every topic in this stage, with code examples: Python Data Science Handbook, chapter 5.
  • Explainability, at length: the free book Interpretable Machine Learning.

Goalthe full project on GitHub, with a README that explains why you chose the metric and the final model.

Stage 5Neural networks

A neural network is a function made of many layers of simple operations (matrix multiplications followed by a small nonlinearity), with millions or billions of parameters. It is still trained with gradient descent, and the gradient for each parameter is computed with the chain rule, applied layer by layer from the end back to the beginning. This is called backpropagation, and it is the central idea of the stage. To really understand it, you first write it yourself from scratch, then move to PyTorch, the library used by almost every researcher and engineer in the field.

Steps, in order

  1. What a neural network is and how it learns. The Neural networks playlist by 3Blue1Brown, the first four chapters: But what is a neural network?, Gradient descent, Backpropagation, intuitively, Backpropagation calculus.
  2. Play with a network in the browser. On TensorFlow Playground, change the number of layers and neurons and watch how it learns to separate the points. Try to solve the spiral.
  3. Backpropagation written by you. Video: building micrograd (Andrej Karpathy, the first in the Neural Networks: Zero to Hero series). Write the code along with him in Colab, pausing the video often. It is long (2h25m) and it is the most important step in the stage.
  4. Your first model trained with PyTorch. From the same series: building makemore and makemore Part 2: MLP. You build a model that invents new names and learn about the training loop, the learning rate and splitting data into training, validation and test sets.
  5. PyTorch, systematically. The official Learn the Basics tutorial: tensors, datasets, building a network, training, saving. In Colab, choose Runtime, then Change runtime type, then GPU, to see the difference in speed.
  6. Networks for images (CNNs). The videos But what is a convolution? and Image Classification with CNNs, then on Kaggle, in Digit Recognizer, train a network in PyTorch that recognizes handwritten digits.
  7. The practical, top-down approach. The Practical Deep Learning for Coders course (fast.ai), lessons 1-3: you train an image classifier on photos you choose, publish it as a web app on Hugging Face Spaces and see what happens inside it.
  8. Why training sometimes fails. Video: makemore Part 3: Activations & Gradients, BatchNorm. You learn to look inside a network during training and recognize common problems.

If something is unclear

  • Neural networks once more, more slowly: The Essential Main Ideas of Neural Networks (StatQuest).
  • PyTorch, step by step, with exercises: the free course Learn PyTorch for Deep Learning.
  • If you prefer reading: the free book Understanding Deep Learning, with very clear figures, or Dive into Deep Learning, with code for every chapter.

Goalmicrograd rewritten by you without the video, a network that recognizes more than 98% of the Digit Recognizer digits, and a model published on Hugging Face Spaces.

Stage 6Deep learning in depth

A small network almost trains itself; a large one does not. This stage is about the tricks that make the difference: optimizers that are better than plain gradient descent, methods that stop the network from memorizing, architectures that allow tens or hundreds of layers, and reusing models that are already trained. At the end you also see recurrent networks (RNNs), which were the standard for text before transformers.

Steps, in order

  1. How to train a network in practice, step by step. The article A Recipe for Training Neural Networks (Karpathy). Reread it after each step below.
  2. Backpropagation done by hand on a real network, and a deeper architecture. The videos makemore Part 4: Becoming a Backprop Ninja and makemore Part 5: Building a WaveNet.
  3. Optimizers (SGD with momentum, Adam) and the learning rate. The Optimization and Learning and Evaluation notes from Stanford's CS231n course.
  4. The rest of the fast.ai course. From Practical Deep Learning for Coders, lessons 4-8: text, a model written from scratch, random forests, recommendations and convolutions. Along the way you meet dropout and weight decay, the two regularization methods used everywhere.
  5. Very deep networks. The Residual Networks (ResNet) chapter of Dive into Deep Learning. You will find the idea of residual connections again in every transformer.
  6. Reusing a model trained by someone else (transfer learning). The Transfer Learning notes from CS231n, then the Computer Vision course on Kaggle Learn. The course uses Keras, a different library from PyTorch, but the ideas are the same.
  7. Networks for sequences (text, sound, time series). The videos Recurrent Neural Networks and LSTM (StatQuest), then the Recurrent Neural Networks chapter of Dive into Deep Learning. You will see why something better was needed, namely the transformers of the next stage.
  8. Project. Pick an image problem that interests you, start from a pre-trained model and adapt it to your data. Keep an experiment log: what you changed, what happened to the error and why you think it happened.

If something is unclear

  • A full, slower course with assignments: Deep Learning Specialization (Andrew Ng, Coursera). Enrolling is free; the certificate is paid.
  • If you prefer reading: Understanding Deep Learning, chapters 6-11.

Goalthe project with its experiment log on GitHub, and being able to explain why Adam, dropout and residual connections help training.

Stage 7Transformers

Language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT, Gemini or Llama are very large neural networks of the transformer type, trained to guess the next piece of text. The new ingredient compared to the previous stages is attention, the mechanism by which each word "looks at" the others to understand its meaning in context. Transformers are now also used for images, sound and proteins, so this stage is the foundation for everything that follows. You finish it with a small GPT, written and trained by you.

Steps, in order

  1. The big picture. Short video: Large Language Models explained briefly (3Blue1Brown).
  2. How words become numbers (embeddings). Video: Word Embedding and Word2Vec (StatQuest). In short: each word becomes a vector, and words with similar meanings end up as nearby vectors.
  3. How a transformer works. Chapters 5-7 of the 3Blue1Brown playlist: Transformers, the tech behind LLMs, Attention in transformers, How might LLMs store facts.
  4. The same thing, seen from the inside. Open Transformer Explainer, which runs a small GPT in the browser and shows you every computation, then read The Illustrated Transformer.
  5. A GPT built by you. Video: Let's build GPT: from scratch, in code, spelled out (Karpathy). Write the code in Colab, with a GPU, and train a model that writes text in the style of Shakespeare.
  6. How text is cut into tokens (tokenization), and why this explains many of the strange mistakes LLMs make, such as counting the letters in a word. Video: Let's build the GPT Tokenizer (Karpathy).
  7. Pre-trained models, with Hugging Face, where almost all open models are published. From the LLM Course, chapters 1 and 2: what transformers can do, which types exist (encoder, decoder) and how to use them with the Transformers library.
  8. The original paper, now that you can understand it: Attention Is All You Need. It is the first paper in this guide; you do not read it line by line, but compare the figure showing the architecture with your code from step 5.

If something is unclear

  • The same topic, more slowly: Transformer Neural Networks, Clearly Explained (StatQuest).
  • If you prefer reading: the chapter on transformers in Understanding Deep Learning.

Goalthe small GPT you trained on GitHub, and being able to explain, in your own words, what attention does.

Stage 8How an LLM is trained

An assistant like ChatGPT or Gemini is built in three phases. First, pretraining: the model reads a huge part of the internet and learns to continue any text, which costs millions of dollars in GPUs. Then fine-tuning: it is trained further on conversations written by people, so that it answers like an assistant. Finally, learning from feedback (RLHF and its variants): the model is rewarded for good answers, and this is also how reasoning models learn to "think" step by step before answering. You cannot repeat pretraining at home at a large scale, but you can fine-tune a small model.

The steps below go through the phases in order: pretraining in steps 2 and 3, fine-tuning in step 4, feedback and reasoning in steps 5 and 6.

Steps, in order

  1. The whole story, from start to finish. Video: Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT (Karpathy, 3h30m). It is the map of the stage: each step below goes deeper into one part of it.
  2. Pretraining, in practice. Video: Let's reproduce GPT-2 (124M) (Karpathy). You see everything that changes when you go from a toy model to a real one: lots of data, more GPUs, reduced precision, speed tricks. Watch it and write the code as far as the free Colab GPU allows.
  3. How big the model has to be and how much data it needs (scaling laws). The paper Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models (Chinchilla): read the abstract, the introduction and the figures.
  4. Fine-tuning. From the LLM Course, chapter 3 (Fine-tuning a pretrained model), then chapter 11 (Fine-tune Large Language Models), where you learn fine-tuning on conversations and LoRA: instead of changing billions of parameters, you train only a few small matrices added on top of them (the LoRA paper).
  5. Learning from feedback. The video RLHF, Clearly Explained (StatQuest), then the article Illustrating RLHF on Hugging Face. Finally, the abstract of the DPO paper, the simpler variant that is very widely used today.
  6. Reasoning models. From the LLM Course, chapter 12 (Build Reasoning Models): how a model learns to solve math and programming problems through trial and reward.
  7. How you know whether an LLM is good. Hugging Face's LLM Evaluation Guidebook: benchmarks, human evaluation, evaluation by another model, and the pitfalls of each.
  8. Running models efficiently. The Quantization page in the Transformers documentation explains how a model is shrunk so it fits on a laptop. Then install Ollama and run a small open model locally.
  9. Project. In Colab, take a small open model, adapt it with LoRA on a dataset you build yourself (for example, questions and answers in your own language on a topic you are passionate about), evaluate it before and after, and publish it on the Hugging Face Hub.

If something is unclear

  • A full, very deep course with assignments where you write everything from scratch: Stanford's CS336, Language Modeling from Scratch, with the lectures recorded on YouTube. It is hard; it is for after you finish this stage.
  • Fine-tuning, more practical and at a slower pace: a smol course on Hugging Face.
  • The whole path, on a small model, in a single code project: nanochat (Karpathy). The full training run needs rented GPUs, so it costs money; reading the code is free.

Goalyour LoRA-adapted model published on the Hugging Face Hub, and being able to explain the difference between pretraining, fine-tuning and RLHF.

Stage 9Generative and multimodal models

So far your models classified or predicted something. Generative models create new things: images, sound, video. The most widely used today are diffusion models, which start from random noise and clean it up step by step until it becomes an image. Multimodal models connect several types of data, for example text and images, which lets them draw from a description or describe a photo.

Steps, in order

  1. The big picture. Video: But how do AI images and videos actually work? (Welch Labs, on the 3Blue1Brown channel). It explains both diffusion and the link between text and images (CLIP).
  2. The first idea of a generative model: compress an image into a small vector and reconstruct it (autoencoder), then generate new images from randomly chosen vectors (VAE). The article From Autoencoder to Beta-VAE, up to and including the section on VAEs.
  3. Two networks competing: one generates, the other guesses whether it is fake (GAN). Google's short course Generative Adversarial Networks.
  4. Diffusion, intuitively. The video How AI Image Generators Work (Computerphile), then the article The Illustrated Stable Diffusion.
  5. Diffusion in code. The Diffusion Models Course on Hugging Face, units 1-3: a diffusion model written from scratch, then conditioning on a class or a text, then Stable Diffusion.
  6. Transformers for images, and multimodal models. From the Computer Vision Course, Unit 3 (Vision Transformers) and Unit 4 (Multimodal Models).
  7. Sound: speech recognition and speech generated from text. From the Audio Course, units 1, 2, 5 and 6.
  8. Project. Train a small diffusion model in Colab on an image dataset of your choice (for example, logos or pixel art) and publish it as a demo on Hugging Face Spaces.

If something is unclear

  • The math behind diffusion models, in full: What are Diffusion Models? (Lilian Weng).
  • Everything built from scratch, in more than 30 hours of video: the second part of the fast.ai course, which rebuilds Stable Diffusion starting from matrix multiplication.

Goalyour diffusion model published on Hugging Face Spaces, and being able to explain, in your own words, how a model gets from noise to an image that matches a text.

Stage 10Reinforcement learning

In reinforcement learning (RL) there are no examples with the correct answer. An agent takes actions in an environment (a game, a robot, a conversation), gets a reward or a penalty, and learns by trial and error which policy brings the highest reward in the long run. This is how we got AlphaGo, robots that walk and, more recently, the reasoning LLMs from Stage 8.

Steps, in order

  1. What RL looks like in practice. Video: Training AI to Play Pokemon with Reinforcement Learning. Pay special attention to how hard it is to choose the right reward.
  2. The concepts and your first agent. The Deep RL Course on Hugging Face, Unit 1: state, action, reward, policy, and an agent trained to land a spacecraft (LunarLander).
  3. The vocabulary, in writing. Part 1: Key Concepts in RL from Spinning Up.
  4. The first algorithms. From the Deep RL Course, Unit 2 (Q-learning, with a table, written by you from scratch) and Unit 3 (Deep Q-learning, where the table is replaced by a neural network, on Atari games).
  5. Another family of algorithms, which learn the policy directly. From the Deep RL Course, the units on policy gradient, actor-critic and PPO. PPO is also the algorithm used in RLHF.
  6. Your own environment. With Gymnasium, the standard library for RL environments, write a simple game (for example, a snake on a 10 × 10 board) and train an agent to play it. Plot how the reward grows during training.

If something is unclear

  • The theory, in full, as video lectures: Introduction to Reinforcement Learning (David Silver, DeepMind and UCL).
  • The field's reference book, free: Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (Sutton and Barto).

Goalthe agent that plays your game on GitHub, with the reward chart, and being able to explain the difference between Q-learning and policy gradient.

Stage 11LLM applications

Most new AI jobs are not about training models, but about building products on top of existing ones: a chatbot that knows a company's documents, a program that extracts data from invoices, an assistant for programmers. Here you learn to talk to an LLM from code, to give it the information it needs and, just as important, to measure how well the application works.

Steps 4 and 5 explain the diagram: embeddings make it possible to search by meaning, and RAG puts the pieces it finds into the prompt.

Steps, in order

  1. Your first call to an LLM from Python. The Getting started guide in Google's Gemini API documentation: the API has a free tier, which is enough for the exercises in this stage. As an alternative, run a model locally with Ollama, which is used from code in almost the same way.
  2. How to write good instructions for a model (prompt engineering). The Prompt Engineering Guide site, which describes the techniques one by one, with examples. Try each technique on the same problem and compare the answers.
  3. An LLM that calls functions you wrote (tool use): the model does not just answer, it can ask for a function to be run, for example one that looks up the weather. The page Function calling with the Gemini API. It is the foundation of Stage 12.
  4. Semantic search: searching by meaning, not by words. The getting-started examples in Sentence Transformers: turn sentences into vectors and find the ones closest to a question.
  5. RAG: first you find the relevant pieces of your documents and give them to the model along with the question, so it answers from them, not from memory. The video What is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)?, then the Advanced RAG tutorial from the Open-Source AI Cookbook on Hugging Face, which shows how to improve the search.
  6. How you measure whether the application works. The article Your AI Product Needs Evals (Hamel Husain).
  7. What can go wrong: prompt injection (text that tricks the model into ignoring its instructions), data leaks, made-up answers. The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications list.
  8. An interface in a few lines. The Gradio Quickstart guide.
  9. Project. A chatbot that answers from your notes from the previous stages: search with embeddings, RAG, a Gradio interface, and a set of 20 test questions with the expected answers, which you run after every change. Publish it on Hugging Face Spaces.

If something is unclear

  • Short courses on almost every topic in this stage: DeepLearning.AI Courses. The videos are free, while labs, quizzes and certificates require a Pro subscription.

Goalthe chatbot published and the test set on GitHub, with the score before and after each improvement.

Stage 12Agentic AI

An agent is an LLM put in a loop: it gets a goal, decides which tool to use (a search, a file, a program), sees the result and decides the next step, until the task is done. The difference from a chatbot is that an agent acts, not just answers: coding agents like Aider or GitHub Copilot read an entire project, write code, run the tests and fix their own mistakes. The stage starts from an agent you write in a few dozen lines and goes on to multi-agent systems, the standard agents use to connect to tools (MCP), and how to evaluate agents and make them safe.

In step 3 you write exactly this loop yourself, and MCP, from step 5, is the standard the agent uses to connect to tools.

Steps, in order

  1. What an agent is and what it is made of: planning, memory, tools. The article LLM Powered Autonomous Agents (Lilian Weng), then the ReAct page, the idea of alternating reasoning with actions that almost all agents are built on.
  2. When you need an agent and when a fixed workflow is enough. The Workflows and agents page in the LangGraph documentation. Remember the patterns (prompt chaining, routing, orchestrator-worker) and the main advice: start with the simplest solution.
  3. Your first agent, without any special library. Using the tool use from Stage 11, write the agent loop in Python: send the message, if the model asks for a tool run it and send back the result, and repeat until it answers. Give it three tools (a calculator, reading a file, listing a folder) and ask it to summarize a folder of notes.
  4. Good context. The article Context Engineering on the LangChain blog. You learn what information to give the agent at each step, why a tool's name and description matter as much as the prompt, and what to do when the conversation gets too long.
  5. MCP (Model Context Protocol), the open standard that lets any agent connect to any tool or data source. The Introduction page, then the Build an MCP server tutorial, where you write your own server and connect it to an assistant. In depth: the MCP Course on Hugging Face.
  6. Libraries for agents. The AI Agents Course on Hugging Face, from start to finish: agents with smolagents, LlamaIndex and LangGraph, an agentic RAG use case and a final project with a certificate.
  7. Multi-agent: several agents working together. The Multi-agent page in the LangChain documentation: a main agent splits the task among specialized subagents. You also learn when the extra complexity is worth it, because more agents mean more calls and higher costs.
  8. Coding agents. Install Aider, an open source coding agent that runs in the terminal and also works with free models, and use it on one of your projects so far, following the Tips page. Also look at SWE-bench, the standard test used to compare coding agents: real issues from open source projects.
  9. How to evaluate an agent when the same goal can be reached in several ways. From the AI Agents Course, the bonus unit AI Agent Observability and Evaluation.
  10. Agent safety. An agent that reads outside content, has access to private data and can send data out can be tricked by hidden text into sending that data to someone. The article The lethal trifecta (Simon Willison) explains why, and how to defend against it.
  11. Project. An agent that solves a real problem of yours (for example, it organizes your notes and makes you a review plan, or looks for sources and writes a summary with links), with at least one tool exposed through an MCP server you wrote, a set of 10 test tasks and clear rules about what it may do without asking you.

If something is unclear

  • The original ReAct paper, for the details: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models.
  • Agents built as graphs of steps, with fine control over each step: the LangGraph documentation.
  • Short courses on agents, MCP and specific libraries: DeepLearning.AI Courses. The videos are free, while labs, quizzes and certificates require a Pro subscription.

Goalyour agent and MCP server on GitHub, with the results on the 10 test tasks, and being able to explain when you would use an agent and when a fixed workflow.

Stage 13MLOps and production

A model that only lives in a notebook is of no use to anyone. To be used by real people, it has to run as a service and be possible to retrain and reproduce, and someone has to notice when it starts making mistakes (for example, because the data in the world has changed). All of this is called MLOps, and it is a large part of an ML engineer's work.

Steps, in order

  1. What an ML system in production looks like. From the Machine Learning Crash Course, the Production ML systems module.
  2. Applications that run the same way on any computer. Docker's Get started guide.
  3. Your model as a web service. The FastAPI tutorial, the first sections, then put your House Prices model behind an endpoint that receives a house's data and returns its price.
  4. Experiments you can reproduce: which data, which code and which settings produced each result. The getting-started guide in the MLflow documentation.
  5. The whole cycle, explained from start to finish. The Made With ML course, the sections Design, Data, Model, Developing, Testing, Reproducibility and Production.
  6. The same path, with a guided project. MLOps Zoomcamp: experiment tracking, orchestration, deployment, monitoring. You can do it on your own at any time, or together with other learners when a new cohort starts.
  7. Project. Take one of your models and carry it all the way: experiments in MLflow, a FastAPI service in Docker, tests run automatically on GitHub on every change, and a small report that flags when the incoming data starts to differ from the training data.

If something is unclear

  • The Full Stack Deep Learning course, with video lectures on everything involved in building products with deep learning and LLMs.
  • A map of MLOps concepts: ml-ops.org.

Goalthe full project on GitHub, which someone else can start with a single command.

Stage 14Ethics, safety and interpretability

A model learns everything in the data, including the biases, and a model used by millions of people multiplies them. Beyond that, no one knows exactly what happens inside an LLM: interpretability is the field that tries to find out.

Steps, in order

  1. Bias and responsibility. The Intro to AI Ethics course on Kaggle Learn, then the Fairness module of the Machine Learning Crash Course.
  2. The law. The European AI Act applies across the EU, including Romania. From the summary on artificialintelligenceact.eu, find out which systems are banned, which are high-risk and what obligations the people who build them have.
  3. How an LLM gets values and rules of behavior. The Model Spec document, published by OpenAI, describes how their models should behave and how they decide between rules that contradict each other.
  4. What happens inside an LLM. On Neuronpedia, explore the concepts found inside some open models, then work through Chapter 1: Transformer Interpretability of the free ARENA curriculum.
  5. The major risks of advanced AI and how people are working on them. The free online courses from BlueDot Impact, where you go through the materials in a small group, with a facilitator.
  6. Project. Take a model you trained (for example, the Titanic one) and check whether it makes mistakes more often for one group than for another. Write one page on what you found, where you think the difference comes from and what you could do about it.

If something is unclear

  • Explainability of classical models, as a recap: Interpretable Machine Learning.

Goalthe analysis from step 6 on GitHub, and being able to explain which AI Act risk category each of your projects would fall into.

Stage 15Choosing a direction

After the stages so far, you have already tried a little of every AI job. In this last stage you learn to keep up with a field that changes from one month to the next, take part in a real competition through to the end, and choose what to focus on next, based on what you enjoyed most. The table below summarizes them.

Direction What it does Most important stages Where to continue What matters when hiring
Data scientist Analyzes data and builds models that help with decisions 3, 4 Kaggle Competitions Projects, competition results, solid statistics
ML engineer / MLOps Takes models to production and keeps them running 4, 6, 13 MLOps Zoomcamp, Full Stack Deep Learning Good programming, cloud, a project taken all the way to production
AI engineer (applications and agents) Builds products on top of LLMs: RAG, agents, and their evaluation 11, 12, 13 Your own projects, contributions to open source projects with agents or MCP Published applications, with evaluations
LLM engineer Trains and adapts language models 7, 8 CS336, smol course Models published on Hugging Face, experience with GPUs
Computer vision / generative AI Models for images, video, sound 6, 9 Computer Vision Course, fast.ai part two Projects and competition results
Reinforcement learning / robotics Agents that learn by trial and error 10 Deep RL Course, Spinning Up Math and projects; usually a master's or PhD
Research (including safety and interpretability) Invents new methods and publishes papers all, plus 14 Papers reproduced in code, ARENA A master's or PhD, published papers

Steps, in order

  1. AI beyond neural networks: search, logic, probability. Harvard's CS50 AI course, the lectures Search and Uncertainty, each with its final project.
  2. How to read a paper without getting lost. How to Read a Paper (S. Keshav), three pages: reading in three passes.
  3. How to keep up. Once a week, look at Daily Papers on Hugging Face and pick a single paper, which you read with the method from step 2.
  4. A real competition. Pick an active competition on Kaggle and take part until it ends, reading the other participants' notebooks and discussions along the way.
  5. The direction. Pick a row in the table and start the course in the Where to continue column.

Whatever direction you choose

  • A GitHub portfolio, with a clear README for every project in this guide, matters more than any certificate. Certifications are not required at the start.
  • If you are still in high school, it is worth looking at the International Olympiad in Artificial Intelligence (IOAI). If you are a university student, look at the EEML summer school, where researchers from major AI labs teach.

Goalyour first Kaggle competition taken through to the end and a direction chosen, with the next course already started.

Good habits and communities

In the long run, a few habits kept up consistently matter more than any particular course.

  • Write the code yourself, do not copy it. With Karpathy's videos and with tutorials, pause and write every line; a few days later, try to rewrite the code from memory.
  • Keep an experiment log: what you changed, what result you got, what you think it means. In ML, most of the time goes into experiments that do not work, and the log helps you not repeat them.
  • Learn in public. Put every project on GitHub with a short README and, from time to time, write an explanation of something you recently understood. When you explain something to someone else, you are forced to really understand it.
  • Use AI assistants as teachers: ask them for explanations, examples and a check of your reasoning, not for solutions. On projects, first write a version on your own, then compare it with what the assistant suggests.
  • Check any important number or claim that comes from an LLM, including claims about AI. Models sometimes make things up with great confidence.
  • Communities where you can ask questions and learn from others: Kaggle Discussions, the Hugging Face Discord server, r/learnmachinelearning and, if you are in Romania and want in-person meetups, Bucharest AI on Meetup. Many universities also have AI clubs for students.
